title: What is a corporate bond?
subtitle: A company borrowing directly from investors, bypassing banks
openingQuestion: Why might a large company choose to issue bonds instead of borrowing from a bank?
openingOptions: Issuing bonds reaches many investors at once, raising a large amount of capital with more flexible terms
Because bonds don't require paying interest
Because bonds are always cheaper than a bank loan in every case
Because banks won't lend to large companies
explanation: A corporate bond is a debt instrument a company issues directly to investors (no bank as intermediary). It allows raising capital at scale, diversifying funding sources, and sometimes costs less than a bank loan if the company has a strong credit rating.

diagram.label: It issues bonds and sells them directly to investors
No bank intermediary, and a larger scale is possible
Its yield is always higher than a government bond of the same maturity

realWorldExample.description: Apple regularly issues corporate bonds despite holding hundreds of billions of dollars in cash - taking advantage of low rates to fund share buybacks rather than repatriating overseas cash and paying tax on it.

quiz.question: Why does a corporate bond always yield more than a government bond of the same maturity?
options: Because any company carries higher default risk than the government
Because companies must pay tax on their coupon interest
Because corporate bonds always have longer maturities than usual
Because regulators set a floor interest rate for this group of bonds
quiz.explanation: Any company (with vanishingly rare exceptions) carries higher default risk than a government → it must always pay a positive credit spread over the risk-free rate. How large that spread is depends on that company's own credit rating.

quiz.question: Why can the interest rate on bonds from the same company differ significantly by maturity (5-year, 10-year, 30-year), even when the company's credit risk hasn't changed?
options: Because the credit rating is reassessed separately for each maturity
Because each maturity sits at a different point on the yield curve
Because long-maturity bonds must be backed by collateral
Because issuance costs scale with the number of years, making longer maturities pricier
quiz.explanation: Corporate bond yield = risk-free rate (at the matching point on the yield curve) + credit spread (reflecting the company's own credit risk) - both components can shift with maturity, which is why the overall rate can differ noticeably across a company's own maturities.

quiz.question: What two parts make up a corporate bond's yield?
options: The inflation rate plus the company's growth rate
The policy rate plus the issuer's profit margin
The risk-free rate at the same maturity plus a credit spread
The deposit rate plus an underwriting fee
quiz.explanation: Separating these two parts is genuinely useful when you read the news: a rising yield can come from rates in general rising, or from the company's own credit deteriorating - two different causes leading to two very different investment conclusions.

quiz.question: Why would a company issue bonds instead of simply borrowing from a bank?
options: To avoid being bound by any restrictive covenants at all
To avoid periodic disclosure requirements
To get a lower rate than a bank loan in every case
To raise a larger amount of capital and diversify its funding sources
quiz.explanation: A bank has a lending limit for each client; the bond market pools capital from thousands of investors, so the scale is far larger. In exchange, the company takes on tighter disclosure obligations and more market discipline.

quiz.question: For the same company, a 30-year bond yields more than a 5-year bond. Why?
options: Because both the base rate and credit uncertainty widen with time
Because the company's credit rating steadily declines over the years
Because long-maturity bonds are far more liquid
Because the company must pay far more coupon periods over thirty years
quiz.explanation: Two forces point the same way: the yield curve usually slopes upward, and predicting a company will still be healthy in thirty years is much harder than in five. Both the base rate and the risk premium widen.

keyTakeaways: Corporate bond: a company borrowing directly from investors
Advantage: raises large amounts of capital and diversifies funding beyond banks
Always carries a positive credit spread over a government bond of the same maturity

practicePrompt.question: A company needs to raise 500 billion VND to expand a factory. Instead of a bank loan, it issues bonds and sells them directly to investors in the market. What is this form of fundraising called, and how does it differ from a traditional bank loan?
options: This is called an IPO, since the company is raising capital from the public to expand its operations
Corporate bond: borrowing directly from many investors, with no bank as intermediary
This is called a buyback, since the company is repurchasing part of its capital from investors
A corporate bond and a bank loan are entirely identical, just different names for the same thing
practicePrompt.explanation: Corporate bond: a company borrowing directly from investors (no bank intermediary as in a traditional loan). The interest rate depends on the company's credit rating - a riskier company must pay a higher rate to attract investors.

summary.keyIdea: Corporate bond: a company borrowing directly from investors
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Advantage: raises large amounts of capital and diversifies funding beyond banks

application.title: Compare a corporate bond with a Treasury
application.message: The lesson already worked a real example using the 10-year government bond yield (4.11%/year) as the anchor - see the 'Real example' section above. Now find a corporate bond of the same maturity to compare against it.
application.secondary: The wider the gap, the more the market doubts that company's ability to repay its debt.

sections.text: When a company needs a large amount of capital, it has two main choices: borrow from a bank, or issue a corporate bond - borrowing directly from thousands of investors in the market, with no bank as intermediary.
Why a company issues bonds instead of just borrowing from a bank

Issuing bonds allows raising a large amount of capital at once, diversifies funding sources beyond banks, and for a company with a strong credit rating, can sometimes even cost less than a traditional bank loan. An interesting example: Apple regularly issues corporate bonds despite holding hundreds of billions of dollars in cash - the reason being to take advantage of low rates to fund its share buyback program, rather than repatriating cash held overseas and paying tax on it.
Corporate bond yield = risk-free rate + credit spread

Any company - however strong - carries higher default risk than a government, so a corporate bond must always pay a positive credit spread over a government bond of the same maturity. But a corporate bond's yield does not depend only on the credit spread - it also depends on where that maturity sits on the yield curve. That is why, for the same company, 5-year, 10-year, and 30-year bonds can carry meaningfully different rates even when the company's credit risk hasn't changed: total yield = risk-free rate (at the matching maturity) + credit spread (based on the company's rating).

items: Corporate bond: a company borrowing directly from investors, with no bank as intermediary
Advantage: raises large amounts of capital, diversifies funding, sometimes costs less than a bank loan
Always carries a positive credit spread over a government bond of the same maturity
Rates differ by maturity, even for bonds issued by the same company

sections.text: Real example: using the government bond yield as an anchor

items: The 10-year Vietnam government bond: a winning auction yield of about 4.11%/year (2026 data) - close to risk-free
A corporate bond of the same maturity typically requires a yield 3-7 percentage points (300-700 basis points) higher, depending on the issuer's credit risk
That gap (the spread) is exactly the "reward" investors demand to compensate for the risk the company fails to repay its debt

sections.label: How to compare against a real corporate bond yourself
sections.text: Look up the government bond yield at the matching maturity on VBMA (vbma.org.vn, Government Bond Auction Results section) or HNX, then set it beside the issuance/trading yield of a corporate bond at the same maturity to calculate a real spread yourself.
